<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsubsection"><a href="#S4.SS3.SSS4" title="In 4.3 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.3.4 </span>Attention-Based Interpretability Metrics</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
</ol></li>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data.
This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control.
We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution.
We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced.
Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities.
We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns.
Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;">
</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) process all tokens in a context window through the same attention mechanism, without any built-in distinction between executable instructions, passive data, and auxiliary context <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaddour et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
This architectural uniformity means that any token can equally influence model behavior, whether it originates from a user instruction, a retrieved document, or an injected adversarial payload.
The practical consequences are well-documented: prompt injection attacks that hijack model execution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Greshake et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez and Ribeiro, 2022</a>)</cite>, ambiguous referential binding when multiple instructions coexist in context (e.g., “execute the second task”), and degraded reliability in compositional scenarios involving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and tool calling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schick et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
These failure modes stem from a single root cause: the model has no mechanism to distinguish executable instructions from passive data at the token level.
Current instruction-tuning approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>)</cite> train models to follow instructions implicitly, based on position, formatting conventions (e.g., “chat templates”), and statistical patterns, thus lack the mechanism to distinguish which instruction to execute when multiple candidates exist in a given prompt.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we present a structured post-training methodology built on LLMON <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hind et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">LLMON Team, 2026</a>)</cite> (LLM Object Notation), a hierarchical tagging framework that introduces explicit instruction-data separation and identifier-based execution binding into the LLM interface.
Under LLMON, each instruction and data segment is wrapped in typed, uniquely identified blocks, and execution occurs only through explicit execution calls that reference specific instruction and data identifiers.
This design steers the model toward a clear semantic principle where only explicitly invoked instructions are executed.
Our contributions are:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We describe a scalable data pipeline that transforms instruction-tuning corpora (general, RAG, and tool-calling) into LLMON-structured training data, including distractor-augmented variants with up to three competing instructions and irrelevant data segments.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct a post-training evaluation on two base models (<span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1-3B-Base</span> and <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1-8B-Base</span>) under full fine-tuning with 4.6B tokens, followed by reinforcement learning.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce attention-based interpretability metrics: Instruction Focus Ratio (IFR), Data Attention Score (DAS), and Leakage (LEAK), to provide mechanistic insight into how structured training reshapes model attention.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Instruction tuning and alignment.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Instruction tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and preference-based alignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christiano et al., 2017</a>)</cite> have become the standard post-training pipeline for modern LLMs.
These methods train models to follow natural-language instructions but rely on implicit positional cues and chat templates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hugging Face, 2025</a>)</cite>-based formatting conventions, rather than explicit structural semantics.
When multiple instructions appear in context, models lack a principled mechanism for disambiguation.
Our work is complementary: LLMON-structured supervision can be applied on top of any instruction-tuning corpus to add explicit execution binding behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Prompt injection and adversarial robustness.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prompt injection exploits the absence of privilege separation between instructions and data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Greshake et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez and Ribeiro, 2022</a>)</cite>.
Spotlighting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hines et al., 2024</a>)</cite> marks untrusted spans with in-band text delimiters at the prompt level, while StruQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> and SecAlign <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> make the boundary a <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">training</em> objective, fine-tuning on structured prompts and preference pairs in which injected instructions are present but must not be followed.
We differ in two respects.
First, the boundary is carried by reserved single tokens from a disjoint region of the vocabulary rather than by in-band delimiters or role names, so it cannot be formed by subword composition of ordinary content.
Second, privilege attaches to an explicit binding rather than to a role: every span is individually addressable and authority follows from which pointer references it, so several same-role instructions can coexist with only one bound for execution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tool use and function calling.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Modern LLM systems integrate external tools through structured generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schick et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patil et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
These approaches define tool schemas and train models to emit structured calls, but the instruction-data boundary within the prompt remains implicit.
LLMON’s execution semantics are orthogonal and compatible with tool-calling pipelines: tool definitions, retrieved documents, and user instructions each occupy typed segments with distinct identifiers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Structured generation and constrained decoding.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Constrained decoding approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Willard and Louf, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beurer-Kellner et al., 2023</a>)</cite> enforce output structure at inference time through grammar-based token masking.
Prompting frameworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khattab et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">POML, 2025</a>)</cite> and programming-language abstractions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dantanarayana et al., 2025</a>)</cite> orchestrate LLM calls, and markup-based prompt languages impose document structure on the prompt, but none of these modifies the model’s internal representation of instruction-data boundaries.
Unlike these inference-time or application-layer approaches, LLMON operates at the <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">training data</em> level, teaching models to internalize structural distinctions through supervised learning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Using LLMON (LLM Object Notation)</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section describes how we leverage LLMON <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hind et al., 2026</a>)</cite> to construct structured post-training data that teaches models explicit execution control.
LLMON is a hierarchical tagging framework that introduces instruction-data separation and identifier-based execution binding at the token level, operating within standard autoregressive language modeling without architectural modification.
We briefly summarize the notation relevant to our training methodology, then describe the data construction pipeline.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Notation Overview</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LLMON defines six special delimiter tokens (“<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|open|&gt;</span>”, “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|close|&gt;</span>”, “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|open_end|&gt;</span>”, “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|self_close|&gt;</span>”, “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|:|&gt;</span>”, “<span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|.|&gt;</span>”) that form a typed tagging system.
The key structural elements relevant to training are:</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Typed segments.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All content is wrapped in identified and tagged blocks.
<em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Instructions</em> carry role qualifiers (“<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">instr&lt;|:|&gt;ID</span>”), <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">data</em> segments hold passive content (“<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">data&lt;|:|&gt;ID</span>”), <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">requirements</em> hold output constraints (“<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">req&lt;|:|&gt;ID</span>”), and <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">documents</em> use nested paths (“<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">doc&lt;|.|&gt;title</span>”, “<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">doc&lt;|.|&gt;text</span>”).
<em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Tool definitions</em> are flattened so that every leaf of the JSON schema becomes its own addressable sub-field (“<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tool&lt;|.|&gt;name</span>”, “<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tool&lt;|.|&gt;parameters&lt;|.|&gt;</span><span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">arg</span><span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|.|&gt;type</span>”), and a tool result returns as a “<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">data</span>” block like any other input.
A <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.16" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">system</em> block (“<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.17" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">system&lt;|:|&gt;ID</span>”) carries authoritative policy and persists across turns.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Execution binding.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An execution block explicitly references which instruction to execute, which data to use as input, and where the output should be placed via identifier references as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ The privilege invariant. ‣ 3.1 Notation Overview ‣ 3 Using LLMON (LLM Object Notation) ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
This design enforces a clear semantic paradigm where multiple instructions can coexist in context without interference, as execution requires referencing a specific identifier regardless of position.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The privilege invariant.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Execution binding yields the invariant our training targets: content reached through “<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec&lt;|.|&gt;instruction</span>” or “<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec&lt;|.|&gt;system</span>” is <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">authoritative</em>, whereas everything reached through “<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec&lt;|.|&gt;input</span>” (data, documents, tool schemas, and tool results) is material to be read, not a command to be followed, however it is phrased.
Blocks that no pointer references are rendered into the context but bound to nothing.
Privilege is therefore a property of the binding rather than of a block’s position or role name, and the delimiters that express it are reserved tokens occupying a disjoint region of the vocabulary, so the structure cannot be formed by subword composition of ordinary content.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S3.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">
<span id="S3.F1.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="width:334.7pt;">
<span id="S3.F1.2.1.1" class="ltx_listing ltx_lstlisting ltx_listing"><span class="ltx_listing_data"><a href="data:text/plain;base64," download="">⬇</a></span>
<span id="lstnumberx1" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|open|&gt;</span><span id="lstnumberx1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span><span id="lstnumberx1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|:|&gt;</span><span id="lstnumberx1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">EXEC_ID</span><span id="lstnumberx1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|close|&gt;</span>
</span>

</span>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Data Construction Pipeline</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We develop an automated pipeline that transforms diverse instruction-tuning data into LLMON-structured training examples.
The pipeline handles three distinct data modalities:</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">General instruction data.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Single-turn and multi-turn conversations are serialized with per-turn instruction blocks, “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” bindings, and assistant data blocks.
Each turn receives unique identifiers, and multi-turn examples chain consecutive “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” cycles.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">RAG and document-grounded data.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Retrieved documents are serialized as typed “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">doc</span>” segments with nested “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">doc&lt;|.|&gt;title</span>” and “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">doc&lt;|.|&gt;text</span>” sub-fields.
The “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” block’s input field references both the user’s data and the relevant document identifiers, teaching the model to ground its response in explicitly referenced context.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tool-calling data.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tool definitions are serialized using flattened path-based notation (e.g., “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tool&lt;|.|&gt;function&lt;|.|&gt;name</span>”, “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tool&lt;|.|&gt;function&lt;|.|&gt;description</span>”).
Tool invocations produce a first “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” cycle (user instruction <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> assistant tool call), followed by a tool-result data block and a second “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” cycle (tool result <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> final assistant response).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Distractor Augmentation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The central innovation in our training data is <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">distractor augmentation</em>: systematically injecting competing instructions and irrelevant data into the context while keeping the “<span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” block pointed at only the target.
This directly trains the model to resolve referential bindings under interference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each base example we generate variants with <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\in\{1,2,3\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\in\{1,2,3\}</annotation></semantics></math> distractor instructions (sampled from the instruction pool, excluding the target) and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m\in\{0,1,2,3\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m\in\{0,1,2,3\}</annotation></semantics></math> irrelevant data segments (sampled from other examples).
The distractor instructions and data occupy their own identified blocks in the context, but the “<span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” block references <em id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">only</em> the original target instruction and data, and the target output is identical across all variants of an example.
Variants are sampled per base example, yielding 8 categories parameterized by whether target data is present and by the distractor and irrelevant-data counts.
A model that keys on the “<span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” block is unaffected by the decoys; one that keys on surface cues such as position or imperative phrasing is penalized by the loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We illustrate one such example with a multi-instruction and multi-data distractors execution in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Multi-instruction and Multi-data Distractors ‣ Appendix A LLMON Examples ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Training Data</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following the pipeline of Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Data Construction Pipeline ‣ 3 Using LLMON (LLM Object Notation) ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, we assemble the LLMON-structured corpus from the sources below, totaling 4.4M examples and 4.6B tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">General SFT data</span>: 3.25M single-turn (2.79B tokens) and 59k multi-turn (120M tokens) examples drawn from the Granite-4.1 post-training SFT corpora.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RAG data</span>: 27k single-turn (45.5M tokens) and 8k multi-turn (17.8M tokens) retrieval-augmented examples from the same corpora.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tool-calling data</span>: 451k single-turn (707M tokens) and 251k multi-turn (562M tokens) function-calling examples from the same corpora.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Alpaca</span>: 52k clean examples <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taori et al., 2023</a>)</cite> (17.2M tokens) plus 103k distractor-augmented variants (39.4M tokens).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dolly</span>: 15k clean examples <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Conover et al., 2023</a>)</cite> (3.3M tokens) plus 30k distractor-augmented variants (16.3M tokens).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompt-injection data</span>: 130k examples (211M tokens) in which an adversarial instruction is planted inside a payload the model is meant to read rather than execute, spanning general (40k), RAG (11k), and tool-calling (80k) modalities.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The general, RAG, and tool-calling examples teach the structural format across single-turn instruction following, multi-turn conversation, document-grounded QA, and tool invocation, and account for 93.6% of all tokens, which is what keeps capability close to the conventionally-tuned baseline.
The Alpaca and Dolly expansions supply the distractor-augmented variants of Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Distractor Augmentation ‣ 3 Using LLMON (LLM Object Notation) ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, expanding 67k base examples into 133k variants.
The prompt-injection examples are the training-time counterpart of the evaluation in Section <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS2" title="4.3.2 Indirect Prompt-Injection Benchmarks ‣ 4.3 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3.2</span></a>: the injected instruction is rendered as a block that no execution pointer references, and the target output is the one that ignores it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For the reinforcement-learning stages we use two further sources: approximately 169k prompts across five sequential policy-optimization stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and two mathematics boosters; and approximately 1k on-policy preference pairs for the final preference-optimization stage, constructed from each model’s own responses at agentic decision points where a tool result carries an injected instruction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Models and Training</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We post-train two base models from the same family and generation at different scales: <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1-3B-Base</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1-8B-Base</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">IBM Granite Team, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Granite Team, 2024</a>)</cite>.
Both are base (pre-trained) checkpoints without prior instruction tuning, so the LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on top of an existing chat format.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Supervised fine-tuning.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first install the six LLMON delimiters in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens by remapping unused vocabulary slots, which avoids growing the vocabulary or resizing the embedding matrix.
We then run full fine-tuning, updating all parameters on the LLMON-serialized corpus: three epochs over 4.4M examples and 4.6B tokens at a sequence length of 4096 tokens, sharded across 8<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>H100 GPUs with FSDP.
We report the final-epoch checkpoint.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reinforcement learning.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Starting from the supervised checkpoint, we run five sequential Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) stages against a reward model over the <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>169k prompts described above, which optimize end behavior directly rather than the token-level target.
A final Direct Preference Optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al., 2023</a>)</cite> (DPO) stage then trains on the <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>1k on-policy injection preference pairs (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>, one epoch, learning rate <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-7}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-7}</annotation></semantics></math>, effective batch size 32).
This stage is placed last so that the general-capability stages, which carry no injection objective, cannot erode the boundary behavior installed earlier.
Unless noted otherwise, results reported as “LLMON” refer to this final SFT<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>GRPO<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>DPO checkpoint.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Evaluation</h3>

<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.1 </span>Standard Benchmarks</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify that LLMON post-training preserves general capabilities, we evaluate across seven categories, reporting the unweighted mean over the benchmarks in each:
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">General</span> (MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, MMLU-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024)</a></cite>, BBH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al. (2023)</a></cite>, AGI-Eval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al. (2024)</a></cite>, GPQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al. (2023)</a></cite>);
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Alignment</span> (IFEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>);
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Math</span> (GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, GSM-Symbolic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mirzadeh et al. (2025)</a></cite>, Minerva Math <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lewkowycz et al. (2022)</a></cite>, DeepMind Math <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saxton et al. (2019)</a></cite>);
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Code</span> (HumanEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2021)</a></cite>, HumanEval+ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a></cite>, MBPP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Austin et al. (2021)</a></cite>, MBPP+ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024a)</a></cite>, MultiPL-E <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cassano et al. (2023)</a></cite>, CRUXEval-O <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al. (2024)</a></cite>);
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tool-Calling</span> (BFCL v3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patil et al. (2025)</a></cite>);
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multilingual</span> (Global-MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al. (2025)</a></cite>, MGSM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al. (2022)</a></cite>, INCLUDE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Romanou et al. (2025)</a></cite>);
and <span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Safety</span> (6-task safety aggregate metric from Tulu3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2026)</a></cite>, AttaQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kour et al. (2023)</a></cite>, SALAD-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2024)</a></cite>).
Each LLMON model is compared against the instruct counterpart at the same scale, trained on the matched chat-template corpus of Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Training Data ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.2 </span>Indirect Prompt-Injection Benchmarks</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Indirect prompt injection is the failure mode the privilege invariant is designed to prevent: a malicious instruction is planted in a data payload, such as a retrieved document or a tool response, rather than supplied by the user.
We evaluate on two published benchmarks that place the injection on different surfaces.
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OPI</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024b)</a></cite> injects into the data of classic NLP tasks and defines the five-attack taxonomy used throughout this evaluation (naive, escape, ignore, fake-completion, and combine), together with the attack-success metric.
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ASB</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2025)</a></cite> moves the attack into an agent’s tool observations, which is the surface that matters for tool-using deployments; we report its observation-injection arm.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We report attack success rate (ASR), the fraction of adversarial prompts in which the injected instruction is followed; lower is better.
For the LLMON models the injected payload arrives inside a “<span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">data</span>” block reached through “<span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec&lt;|.|&gt;input</span>”, so following it would require acting on a span the model was trained to read rather than execute; the instruct baselines receive the same payloads under conventional chat formatting.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.3 </span>Adversarial Red-Teaming</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The two benchmarks above measure known, published attacks.
Separately from them, and going beyond what a fixed benchmark can surface, our security team red-teamed both models with ARES <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nedoshivina et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, a robustness-evaluation harness that expands 808 seed prompts from five datasets (Purple <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhatt et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, Gandalf <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pfister et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and TensorTrust <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Toyer et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for direct attacks; Alpaca and a safety-policy set for indirect ones) into approximately 15k attack prompts by mutating each seed through eight attack strategies organized by attacker sophistication, from basic (asking directly) through intermediate (append, ignore, escape-separation, completion-real, append-and-prepend) to advanced.
The advanced arm is a multi-turn variant of Crescendo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Russinovich et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, in which an attacker model generates each next turn and a judge decides whether the adversarial objective was met; we use DeepSeek-V3.2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as the attacker, <span id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">GPT-OSS</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI et al., 2025</a>)</cite> (120B) as the judge, and a budget of 20 turns.
Results are reported as <em id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">robustness</em> (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\text{ASR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mtext>ASR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\text{ASR}</annotation></semantics></math>), so that higher is better, which is the convention of the harness; note that this is the opposite direction to Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Indirect Prompt Injection ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.4 </span>Attention-Based Interpretability Metrics</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond output-level evaluation, we introduce three per-layer attention metrics designed to provide mechanistic insight into model behavior.
These metrics quantify how attention from the final generated token is distributed across target and distractor spans.
Let <math id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A(S)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A(S)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the total attention mass assigned to a span set <math id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>.
We define <math id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> as the target and distractor instruction spans, respectively, and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> as the corresponding target and distractor data spans.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruction Focus Ratio</span> (IFR) measures the proportion of attention allocated to the target instruction relative to all instruction spans:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{IFR}=\frac{A(\mathcal{I}_{t})}{A(\mathcal{I}_{t})+A(\mathcal{I}_{d})}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>IFR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{IFR}=\frac{A(\mathcal{I}_{t})}{A(\mathcal{I}_{t})+A(\mathcal{I}_{d})}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Similarly, the <span id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Data Attention Score</span> (DAS) quantifies the proportion of attention assigned to the target data relative to all data spans:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{DAS}=\frac{A(\mathcal{D}_{t})}{A(\mathcal{D}_{t})+A(\mathcal{D}_{d})}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>DAS</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{DAS}=\frac{A(\mathcal{D}_{t})}{A(\mathcal{D}_{t})+A(\mathcal{D}_{d})}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, <span id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Leakage</span> (LEAK) is the share of all span attention that reaches distractor content, across both instruction and data spans.
Writing <math id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> for every labeled span in the prompt (the target and distractor instructions and data, together with the structural spans: the execution block, the delimiters, and the remaining prompt), LEAK is</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{LEAK}=\frac{A(\mathcal{I}_{d})+A(\mathcal{D}_{d})}{A(\mathcal{S})}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>LEAK</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{LEAK}=\frac{A(\mathcal{I}_{d})+A(\mathcal{D}_{d})}{A(\mathcal{S})}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS4.p8.1" class="ltx_p">These metrics are computed per layer across all attention heads (averaged over attention heads within each KV group for grouped-query-attention models).
This enables layer-wise failure diagnosis: higher IFR and DAS values indicate stronger focus on task-relevant content, whereas larger LEAK values suggest increased attention allocated to irrelevant or competing information.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results and Discussion</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>General Capabilities</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.1 General Capabilities ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> compares LLMON-structured post-training against the <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> chat-template baselines at both scales under matched full fine-tuning.
The objective here is parity rather than improvement: LLMON training is meant to install an execution-binding behavior, not to make the model better at mathematics or code.
Averaged over the six capability categories, the 3B model is unchanged (66.7 both ways) and the 8B model loses 1.4 points (74.2 to 72.8), with mathematics at 8B the largest single regression (84.1 to 79.6).
LLMON improves on Code and Multilingual at 3B.
Safety improves at both scales, by 8.8 points at 3B and 6.2 at 8B, which is where the structural supervision is expected to show.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Indirect Prompt Injection</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Indirect Prompt Injection ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports attack success rate on the two injection benchmarks of Section <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS2" title="4.3.2 Indirect Prompt-Injection Benchmarks ‣ 4.3 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3.2</span></a>.
On text-level injection (OPI) the attack essentially stops working: ASR falls from 100.0 to 0.1 at 3B and from 96.3 to 0.02 at 8B.
On agentic injection (ASB), where the payload arrives in a tool observation rather than in task data, ASR falls from 99.2 to 5.6 at 3B and from 52.8 to 3.1 at 8B.
These are reductions of roughly <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="17\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17\times</annotation></semantics></math> on agentic injection and three orders of magnitude on text-level injection, and they hold at both scales despite the 8B <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> baseline already being markedly more robust on ASB than the 3B one.
The mechanism is structural rather than a learned refusal: the injected instruction occupies a “<span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">data</span>” block that no execution pointer references, so acting on it would require the model to execute a span it was trained to read.
Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Attention Interpretability Analysis ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a> examines what this looks like inside the network.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T2.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S5.T2.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T2.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="S5.T2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model</span></th>
<th id="S5.T2.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="S5.T2.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training</span></th>
<th id="S5.T2.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S5.T2.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">OPI <math id="S5.T2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></th>

<td id="S5.T2.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">99.2</td></tr>

<th id="S5.T2.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">LLMON</th>

<td id="S5.T2.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S5.T2.2.3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5.6</span></td></tr>

<td id="S5.T2.2.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S5.T2.2.5.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3.1</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>LLMON-structured post-training vs. <span id="S5.T2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> chat-template baselines, measured by <span id="S5.T2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">attack success rate (ASR, %)</span> on two published indirect prompt-injection benchmarks: OPI (text-level injection) and ASB (agentic tool-observation injection). <span id="S5.T2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lower is better</span>: ASR is the fraction of adversarial prompts that succeed, so a smaller value means a more robust model. Best (lowest ASR) per model/benchmark in <span id="S5.T2.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bold</span>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Adversarial Red-Teaming</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Independently of the published benchmarks of Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Indirect Prompt Injection ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>, Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Adversarial Red-Teaming ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports the ARES red-teaming campaign of Section <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS3" title="4.3.3 Adversarial Red-Teaming ‣ 4.3 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3.3</span></a>, which uses its own seed datasets and attack strategies and separates results by where the adversarial instruction enters.
Scores are robustness (<math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\text{ASR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mtext>ASR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\text{ASR}</annotation></semantics></math>), so higher is better.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">On <em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">indirect</em> attacks the gain is large and is what the design predicts: robustness rises from 2.8% to 84.6% at 3B and from 0.7% to 79.8% at 8B, because the payload lands in a span that no execution block designates as an operable instruction.
<em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Direct</em> and <em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">multi-turn</em> attacks also improve, roughly doubling at both scales, but remain far weaker in absolute terms (32-37%).
That asymmetry is expected rather than disappointing.
When the adversarial instruction <em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">is</em> the user’s own instruction there is no instruction-data boundary left to enforce, and an attacker who steers a conversation across twenty turns is not smuggling an instruction past the binding but building towards a request the model accepts on its own terms.
The privilege invariant is therefore a defense against untrusted <em id="S5.SS3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">input</em>, and should be composed with defenses of a different kind rather than relied upon alone.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Adversarial red-teaming with ARES, reported as <span id="S5.T3.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">robustness (<math id="S5.T3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\text{ASR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">ASR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\text{ASR}</annotation></semantics></math>, %)</span>, <span id="S5.T3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">higher is better</span>, the opposite direction to Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Indirect Prompt Injection ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Indirect attacks use StruQ-style payloads planted in input, averaged over in-distribution and out-of-distribution splits (ID: 90.3/83.6, OOD: 79.0/75.9 for 3B/8B); direct attacks place the adversarial instruction in the user turn; multi-turn is a Crescendo variant with a 20-turn budget. Best per model/column in <span id="S5.T3.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bold</span>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Attention Interpretability Analysis</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both the injection reductions and the capability picture are consistent across the two scales tested, so the remainder of this section drills into <em id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> that robustness arises.
Using the per-layer attention metrics defined in Section <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS4" title="4.3.4 Attention-Based Interpretability Metrics ‣ 4.3 Evaluation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3.4</span></a>, we analyze the <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1-3B</span> pair (the LLMON-trained model and its <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> counterpart) on distractor prompts in which several instructions, and in most cases several data segments, coexist while the “<span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” block binds only one pair.
We first report the per-layer behavior on a representative example to expose the mechanism, then aggregate over all examples to verify that the trends are not driven by ordering.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Where the binding lives.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both models are measured at the same layers, and the separation is largest in the late-middle of the stack rather than at the output.
Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Where the binding lives. ‣ 5.4 Attention Interpretability Analysis ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reports the mean of each metric over the distractor examples at five representative layers.
The LLMON-trained model holds a mean IFR of 86-87% at layers 25 and 28 against 26-38% for the <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> model, with mean leakage of 6-9% against 35-45%.
At the final layer both models collapse towards chance (IFR 28.0% vs 17.2%), which is why we report the span distribution at layer 31 rather than at layer 39: the execution binding is a mid-to-late-stack computation, and reading it off the last layer alone would understate it for both models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T4.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
