</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Layer-wise Instruction Focus Ratio.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Layer-wise Instruction Focus Ratio. ‣ 5.4 Attention Interpretability Analysis ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the IFR computed at each transformer layer for both models on a representative distractor example, in which three instructions (“summarize”, “count the words”, “translate”) and two data segments coexist and the “<span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” block binds only the word-counting instruction.
The two models are indistinguishable through the first twenty layers, both fluctuating around 25-45%.
They separate sharply from layer 22: the LLMON-trained model rises into a 55-89% band across layers 25-38, peaking at 89% at layer 28, whereas the <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> model peaks at 62% and spends most of that range below 45%.
The implication is that the binding is not a surface property of the prompt but a computation the network performs, and that LLMON training installs it in a specific region of the stack rather than shifting attention uniformly.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.38120v1/figs/ifr_per_layer.png" id="S5.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/245;" width="476" height="245" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Instruction Focus Ratio (IFR) per transformer layer for the LLMON-trained <span id="S5.F2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1-3B</span> (teal) vs. its <span id="S5.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> counterpart (pink) on a distractor example. The two are indistinguishable through layer 20 and separate sharply from layer 22, with the LLMON model sustaining 55-89% across layers 25-38. Both fall at the final layer.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Layer-wise Distractor Leakage.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Layer-wise Distractor Leakage. ‣ 5.4 Attention Interpretability Analysis ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the complementary LEAK metric across layers.
Both models leak heavily in the first six layers, peaking above 50%, which is consistent with early layers aggregating context indiscriminately.
From layer 7 the LLMON-trained model drops to a 5-25% band and settles below 15% after layer 25, while the <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> model stays in the 20-50% range throughout and rises again in the last ten layers.
Distractor suppression is therefore not a property of the input encoding (where the two models behave alike) but something acquired in the same region of the stack where instruction focus is established.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.38120v1/figs/leak_per_layer.png" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/245;" width="476" height="245" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Distractor leakage (LEAK) per transformer layer. Both models leak heavily in the first six layers; from layer 7 the LLMON-trained model (teal) settles into a 5-25% band while the <span id="S5.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> model (pink) remains between 20% and 50% and rises again in the late layers.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Attention span distribution.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Attention span distribution. ‣ 5.4 Attention Interpretability Analysis ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> presents the per-span attention distribution and the three metrics at layer 31 for both models.
The LLMON-trained model splits its span attention between the target instruction (I-T, 23.4%) and the target data it is bound to (D-T, 23.0%), with 35.6% on the prompt and execution structure and only 5.6% on the largest distractor instruction: IFR = 71.4%, DAS = 72.6%, LEAK = 9.9%.
The <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> model inverts this. Its single largest recipient is a distractor instruction (I-D1, 47.5%), with a second distractor taking 21.8% and the target instruction only 14.5%; target data attention is negligible.
Its metrics record the failure directly: IFR = 17.3%, DAS = 22.1%, LEAK = 49.9%.
The two models receive identical token sequences, so the difference is entirely in what the network does with them.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.38120v1/figs/span_distribution_L31.png" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/196;" width="405" height="196" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Attention metrics and per-span attention distribution at layer 31 for the LLMON-trained <span id="S5.F4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1-3B</span> (left) vs. its <span id="S5.F4.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> counterpart (right). The LLMON model divides its attention between the bound target instruction (I-T) and target data (D-T); the <span id="S5.F4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> model’s largest single recipient is a distractor instruction (I-D1, 47.5%).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Layer-wise Data Attention Score.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Layer-wise Data Attention Score. ‣ 5.4 Attention Interpretability Analysis ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> completes the picture with DAS.
It follows the same shape as IFR: the two models track each other through the first twenty layers, then the LLMON-trained model rises into a 46-94% band across layers 23-38 while the <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> model stays between 14% and 56%.
All three metrics therefore separate in the same region of the stack, which is what one expects if a single mechanism of resolving the execution binding is responsible for all three.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.38120v1/figs/das_per_layer.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/245;" width="476" height="245" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Data Attention Score (DAS) per transformer layer for the LLMON-trained <span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1-3B</span> (teal) vs. its <span id="S5.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instruct</span> counterpart (pink). DAS separates in the same region of the stack as IFR and LEAK, rising into a 46-94% band across layers 23-38 for the LLMON model.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Token-level attention flow.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Token-level attention flow. ‣ 5.4 Attention Interpretability Analysis ‣ 5 Results and Discussion ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> traces how attention is allocated during generation, showing the correlation between each generated token and the KV-cache spans for the LLMON-trained model at layer 31.
The target data span (D-T) activates precisely while the model is quoting the sentence it was asked to count, and falls away once it moves on to report the count; the target instruction span (I-T) carries weight at the opening tokens and again as the answer is formed.
The distractor spans (I-D1, I-D2, D-D1) stay near zero throughout decoding.
This token-resolved view complements the per-layer metrics: the model does not merely arrive at the right binding by the end of the forward pass, it holds it step by step as it produces the answer.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.38120v1/figs/attention_flow.png" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/169;" width="405" height="169" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Attention correlation weights between each generated token (columns, in decoding order) and the KV-cache spans (rows) for the LLMON-trained <span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1-3B</span> at layer 31. Brighter cells indicate stronger attention. The target data span (D-T) activates while the model quotes the sentence it was asked to count, and the distractor spans (I-D1, I-D2, D-D1) remain near zero throughout decoding.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented a structured post-training methodology that uses LLMON’s explicit instruction-data separation and identifier-based execution binding to improve controlled execution in LLMs.
Our evaluation on two <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Granite-4.1</span> base models demonstrates that:
(i) LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6%, without catastrophic degradation on standard capability measures;
(ii) the effect holds at both 3B and 8B scale, and extends to adversarial red-teaming on indirect attacks, though direct and multi-turn attacks remain substantially harder;
and (iii) attention-based interpretability metrics (IFR, DAS, LEAK) provide actionable per-layer failure diagnosis, revealing how structural training reshapes internal attention patterns.
These findings suggest that explicit execution structure can be reliably taught to LLMs through standard post-training, offering a training-time complement to inference-time safety mechanisms.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We discuss several important limitations of this work.
First, our evaluation covers two model scales (3B and 8B) within a single model family and generation.
While LLMON’s structural supervision is architecture-agnostic, it remains to be validated whether the same magnitude of improvement transfers to other pre-training corpora and architectures, and to larger scales where models may already exhibit stronger implicit instruction-following.
Second, LLMON’s delimiter tokens increase context length by approximately 7-15% depending on the example complexity.
We do not systematically quantify the impact on inference latency and throughput, though sequence packing at training time largely amortizes this cost.
Third, the privilege invariant addresses <em id="Sx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">indirect</em> injection, where the adversarial instruction arrives as input.
It offers far less protection when the adversarial instruction <em id="Sx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">is</em> the user’s instruction, since there is then no instruction-data boundary to enforce: red-teaming robustness reaches only 33-37% on direct attacks and 28-37% on multi-turn attacks, against 80-85% on indirect ones, and it is a learned behavior rather than an enforced guarantee: it substantially reduces, but does not eliminate, the chance that an instruction embedded in data is followed, and should be one layer of a defense rather than the only one.
Fourth, while our capability evaluation includes multilingual benchmarks, the LLMON training corpus itself is predominantly English, and we have not characterized how tag overhead behaves on morphologically rich languages or on tasks with very long documents.
Finally, our IFR/DAS/LEAK metrics provide correlation between attention patterns and output quality, but we do not establish a causal mechanism.
Attention weights are an imperfect proxy for information flow in transformers, and the relationship between attention-level metrics and generation-level performance may not be monotonic.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>LLMON Examples</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Multi-instruction and Multi-data Distractors</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ A.1 Multi-instruction and Multi-data Distractors ‣ Appendix A LLMON Examples ‣ Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> illustrates a distractor example: three instructions and two data segments coexist, but the “<span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">exec</span>” block unambiguously binds only one instruction-data pair.
The model must learn to attend selectively to the referenced segments and ignore all others.</p>
</div>

<span id="lstnumberx30" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx30.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter">  </span><span id="lstnumberx30.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|open|&gt;</span><span id="lstnumberx30.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF8000;">exec&lt;|.|&gt;input</span><span id="lstnumberx30.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|close|&gt;</span><span id="lstnumberx30.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF00;">data&lt;|:|&gt;Äî</span><span id="lstnumberx30.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|open_end|&gt;</span>
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx31" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx31.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter">  </span><span id="lstnumberx31.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|open|&gt;</span><span id="lstnumberx31.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF8000;">exec&lt;|.|&gt;output</span><span id="lstnumberx31.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|close|&gt;</span><span id="lstnumberx31.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3E6FF;">assistant&lt;|:|&gt;ðã</span><span id="lstnumberx31.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|open_end|&gt;</span>
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx32" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx32.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|open_end|&gt;</span>
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx33" class="ltx_listingline">
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx34" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx34.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|open|&gt;</span><span id="lstnumberx34.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3E6FF;">assistant&lt;|:|&gt;ðã</span><span id="lstnumberx34.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|close|&gt;</span>
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx35" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx35.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">The</span><span id="lstnumberx35.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter"> </span><span id="lstnumberx35.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">sentence</span><span id="lstnumberx35.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space id="lstnumberx35.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter"> </span><span id="lstnumberx35.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">quick</span><span id="lstnumberx35.9" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter"> </span><span id="lstnumberx35.10" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">brown</span><span id="lstnumberx35.11" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter"> </span><span id="lstnumberx35.12" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">fox</span><span id="lstnumberx35.13" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter"> </span><span id="lstnumberx35.14" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">jumps</span><span id="lstnumberx35.15" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter"> </span><span id="lstnumberx35.16" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">over</span><span id="lstnumberx35.17" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter"> </span><span id="lstnumberx35.18" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">the</span><span id="lstnumberx35.19" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter"> </span><span id="lstnumberx35.20" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">lazy</span><span id="lstnumberx35.21" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter"> </span><span id="lstnumberx35.22" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">dog</span><span id="lstnumberx35.23" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">"</span><span id="lstnumberx35.24" id="lstnumberx35.31" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter">words</span><span id="lstnumberx35.32" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.</span>
</span>
<span id="lstnumberx36" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx36.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBFBF;">&lt;|open_end|&gt;</span><span id="lstnumberx36.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-bg-color:#DCDCDC;">&lt;|end_of_text|&gt;</span>
</span>
</span>
</span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Multi-instruction distractor example. Three instructions and two data segments coexist; the bound target instruction and data are shown in green and yellow, the distractors in lime and light-yellow. The exec block (orange) references only “<span id="A1.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">instr&lt;|:|&gt;íä</span>” with input “<span id="A1.F7.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">data&lt;|:|&gt;Äî</span>”. The model must execute only the word-counting instruction, ignoring the summarization and translation distractors. Other special tokens are highlighted in light-pink.</figcaption>
</figure>

      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
